title: The Instruction Format: Opcode, Operand Fields and Length
quickIdea: A machine instruction is an opcode plus the fields that locate its operands. The format decides how many bits each field gets, and that is the whole of what a 'format' means.
remember: Two parts, always: the opcode says what to do, the operand field says where the data is. The addressing mode is the rule for reading that operand field.
A destination operand can be a register or a memory location. An immediate value can only ever be a source, never a destination.
Fixed-length instructions (a 32-bit RISC word) are decoded in one step; variable-length instructions (x86, 1 to 15 bytes) must be decoded byte by byte.
An address field of n bits can name only 2^n locations, which is why direct addressing caps the address space at the width of that field.
Byte-aligned storage: an instruction of b bits occupies ceil(b/8) bytes, and the rounding up is part of the answer to a program-size question.
The register fields are sized by the register file, not by the opcode: 32 registers cost 5 bits per register field, 64 cost 6.

example.prompt: A 32-bit instruction has a 6-bit opcode, two register fields for a 16-register file, and an immediate field. How wide is the immediate field, and what unsigned range does it hold?
example.work: Each register field is log2(16) = 4 bits, so the two of them take 8. The immediate field is 32 - 6 - 8 = 18 bits. An 18-bit unsigned field holds 0 to 2^18 - 1 = 262143.

gateAngle: GATE tests the format as an arithmetic budget far more often than as a diagram: the immediate width of a fixed word (GATE CSE 2016 Set 2 Q.10), the widest immediate an ADD can carry (GATE CSE 2025 Set 1 Q.27), and the opcode count once an addressing-mode field is carved out (GATE CSE 2024 Set 2 Q.47). All three are the same subtraction, done from a different starting point.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A 16-bit instruction has a 4-bit opcode, one 4-bit register field and one address field. How much memory can the address field name, and what happens to that reach if the machine is byte addressable rather than word addressable?
variations.answer: The address field is 16 - 4 - 4 = 8 bits, so it names 2^8 = 256 locations. Byte addressable that is 256 bytes; word addressable with 2-byte words it is 512 bytes.
variations.why: The field width fixes the number of addressable units, and the unit size then fixes the number of bytes. GATE asks the two halves separately; the mistake is to answer 256 bytes without asking what a location is.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does a fixed-length instruction set decode faster than a variable-length one?
variations.answer: Because the opcode always sits in the same bit positions, so the decoder can read it before it knows how long the instruction is; with variable length the opcode's position depends on the bytes already consumed.
variations.why: This is the design reason RISC fixes the length, and it is the sentence behind the RISC-against-CISC comparison rather than a separate fact.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A machine has 12 instructions, 8 registers and a two-address format in a 12-bit word, with a 4-bit mode field. What is the largest immediate the remaining bits can carry?
variations.answer: 4 bits of opcode (12 instructions needs 4), 3 + 3 bits of registers, 4 bits of mode: 12 - 4 - 6 - 4 = -2, so no bits are left. The format does not fit and one field must shrink.
variations.why: The budget can go negative. GATE has asked for a maximum, but the negative case is the one that exposes whether you are adding the fields or guessing.

trap.what: Reading the operand field as if it were always an address.
trap.why: The field is bits; the mode tells you what those bits mean. In immediate mode they are the value, in register mode they are a register number, in direct mode they are a memory address.
trap.counterexample: In ADD R1, #25 the second field holds the number 25. Nothing is fetched from memory location 25, and the instruction is one word long, not two.

check.question: An instruction set has 41-bit instructions that must be byte aligned. How many bytes does a 100-instruction program occupy?
check.explanation: 41 bits rounds up to ceil(41/8) = 6 bytes per instruction, so 100 x 6 = 600. The 7 wasted bits per instruction are the price of byte alignment.
